Triggers.value: When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

issues.explanation: 'Heavy make-up' is hard to reconcile with this patient's demographics (22-year-old single male auditor) and the rest of the profile unless there is a specific unreported context such as concealment or gender expression. In this profile it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the other items, whereas the other maladaptive strategies center on vigilance, escape, and social evaluation.

vignette: Samir was nineteen when the assault occurred in the climate-controlled archive of a logistics firm, a violation that was never about combat but about the suffocating heat, the sharp tang of industrial disinfectant, and the senior inspector's sudden, unprovoked grab from behind. The moral violation of that authority figure treating him as disposable left a permanent scar, while the chemical sting of the cleaner and the inspector's stale tobacco clung to his memory like a second skin. Now twenty-two and working as an auditor in a downtown office, Samir's past and present are locked in a tight cognitive loop that dictates his every move. His body remains permanently locked in a state of high alert, and this constant physiological readiness actively amplifies his distress. Because his nervous system is chronically tuned to scan for danger, the sudden scent of a colleague's heavy cologne in the audit department, the moral violation of a senior partner casually dismissing a junior analyst's work, or a sudden gesture from a supervisor does not merely remind him of the archive; it instantly floods his awareness with the same panic, transforming a mundane workplace moment into a confirmed threat. This amplified reactivity directly forces him toward his safety behaviors. When the olfactory trigger hits, he immediately pivots toward the nearest hallway, his hand instinctively brushing the doorframe to confirm his escape route, because he cannot tolerate the uncertainty of being trapped. To manage this unyielding physiological readiness, Samir adopts thick, concealing clothing and refuses to sit where his performance might be scrutinized. These strategies, intended to buffer him from surprise, paradoxically keep his threat system chronically overactive. By wearing oversized hoodies and high-collared sweaters even in heated conference rooms, he denies his nervous system the corrective evidence that calm is possible, ensuring his body stays braced for the next violation. Each time he avoids a performance review or steps back from team evaluations, the original humiliation deepens. His avoidance convinces him that he is permanently marked by the assault, and that if someone else had been in his shoes, they would have simply defended themselves or walked away. These crushing self-judgments then dictate his daily retreats. Believing he is irrevocably broken and that his former happiness is lost forever, he refuses to participate in client site visits, telling himself he is too compromised to handle unfamiliar environments. When his ex-partner once texted him asking if he had found peace, the comment acted as a fresh relational trigger that immediately reinforced his core negative appraisal, convincing him that he was irreparably damaged. The more he hides in the periphery, the more his internal narrative hardens into one of permanent humiliation, which in turn guarantees he will remain locked in a cycle of scanning for danger and fleeing from it. Yet, by never testing those spaces, his fear of the unknown grows, making every new trigger feel more potent. Each avoided conversation and every concealed body further convinces him that he is fundamentally unsafe, stripping himself of opportunities to test whether the danger was truly everywhere. At twenty-two, Samir walks into the clinic with a notebook full of crossed-out schedules, his shoulders permanently hunched beneath a heavy wool coat. He hasn't missed a deadline, but he has stopped eating with his colleagues and refuses to work remotely, terrified of losing track of the nearest exit. He finally sought help because the silence in his own apartment had grown louder than the noise of the firm, and he is desperate to stop feeling like a stranger in his own skin. He hopes, quietly, to find a way to walk through a room without counting the doors, even if he isn't sure he deserves the peace he's asking for.
